questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial of a Given Function About a Point
questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)={e}^{\pi x/2}$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot x+(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4})\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1+\frac{\pi }{2}x+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x}$ about $x=5$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=5,$ we plug $a=5$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(5)+{f}^{′}(5)(x-5)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(5)(x-5)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{x} & ⟹ &  & f(5) & =\frac{6}{5} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{1}{25} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{x}^{-3} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(5) & =\frac{2}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =(\frac{6}{5})+(-\frac{1}{25})\cdot (x-5)+(\frac{2}{125})\cdot \frac{1}{2}(x-5)^{2} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-\frac{1}{25}(x-5)+\frac{1}{125}(x-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}}$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}}=(1+x)^{-1/2} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}(1+x)^{-3/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{3}{4}(1+x)^{-5/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+(-\frac{1}{2})x+(\frac{3}{4})\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Coefficient in a Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial
questions.problem: What is the coefficient of $(x-3)^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ at $x=3?$
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(3)+{f}^{′}(3)(x-3)+\frac{{f}^{″}(3)}{2}(x-3)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x-3)^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(3)}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=3.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3) & =-\frac{1}{(3)^{2}}=-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x-3)^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(3)}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{9})=-\frac{1}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)$ at $x=1.$ Do not round the answer.

The coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1)+\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2-x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(2-x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=1.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(1)=-\frac{1}{(2-1)^{2}}=-1.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x-1)^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
